polarity.def: A molecule whose electrons are shared unevenly, so one end carries a partial negative charge and the other a partial positive charge. Water is the classic example.

hydrogen-bond.def: A weak attraction between a partially positive hydrogen atom in one molecule and a partially negative atom, such as oxygen or nitrogen, in another molecule or another part of the same large molecule.

cohesion.def: Water molecules sticking to each other through hydrogen bonds.

adhesion.def: Water molecules sticking to other polar or charged surfaces, such as glass or the walls of plant tubes.

surface-tension.def: The resistance of a liquid's surface to being stretched or broken, caused by cohesion among the molecules at the surface.

specific-heat.def: The energy needed to raise the temperature of one gram of a substance by one degree Celsius. Water's is high, so its temperature changes slowly.

heat-of-vaporization.def: The energy needed to turn one gram of a liquid into a gas. Water's is high, so evaporating water carries a lot of heat away.

solvent.def: The substance that other substances dissolve in. Water dissolves many polar and charged substances, so it is the solvent of most cell chemistry.
